title: UMESH CHAND VS. STATE OF U.P

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1114
Page 1 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026)
Umesh Chand ...Appellant(s)
Versus
State of U.P & Ors. ...Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We have before us a case, doomed from its inception
insofar as justice delivery to the victim is concerned,
consequent to a brutal attack with very grievous injuries, the
aftermath of which is even now suffered by the injured victim.
The diversion from the essential tenets of criminal law began
with the framing of a charge under Section 308 of the Indian
Penal Code, 18601
. The Additional Sessions Judge, Bahraich,
who carried out the trial, was gracious to the accused in
having punished them with a sentence of five years rigorous
imprisonment and a fine of Rs.20,000/- with a default
1
In short 'IPC'

Page 2 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
sentence of one year of simple imprisonment. The High Court
was very indulgent insofar as releasing the accused under
Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 19582
. The
present appeal is filed by the informant, the brother of the
victim against the order of the High Court.
3. We heard Sri L.B. Rai, learned Counsel for the
appellant, Sri Namit Saxena, learned AoR for the State and Sri
Aishvary Vikram, learned AoR for the 2nd and 3rd
respondents, who were the accused before the Trial Court.
4. The allegation, as can be noticed from the narration of
PW1, the first informant, was that the 1
st accused was running
a shop, near which PW1 also opened a similar shop, which
angered the accused. On the fateful day, the victim, the
brother of PW1 was engaged in chores and PW1, along with
his wife was proceeding to the shop when they saw the victim
reach in front of A1's shop. Then A1 and A2 together,
suddenly attacked him mercilessly. A1 was holding a cutting
weapon and A2 had a gun, both of which were used
mercilessly on the victim who fainted due to the injuries. The
2 Hereinafter referred to as 'the PoO Act'

Page 3 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
victim was taken to the Bahraich Hospital immediately and
then PW1 reached the police station to give the complaint.
5. The injuries are grievous and have been specifically
noticed by the High Court in the impugned judgment in
paragraph 9; those in the Injury Report, and in paragraph 10;
those in the Discharge Summary. There are cut injuries and
gunshot wounds which, on a plain look, would fall within the
definition of 'grievous hurt' under Section 320 and not 'hurt'
under Section 319 of the IPC. Section 308 hence ought not to
have been charged, and the offence would clearly fall under
Section 307 of the IPC, especially since on facts, none of the
exceptions under Section 300 applies to the crime proper. It
is not a case of grave and sudden provocation or one of
private defence or a sudden fight and neither are the
perpetrators public servants nor is the defence of consent
raised. Be that as it may, the charge was under Section 308 of
the IPC, and the trial was proceeded with and there is little
we can do at this stage.
6. We are, in this case, especially concerned with the
application of Section 4 of the PoO Act. The High Court having
noticed the grievous injuries observed that the evidence of

Page 4 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
an injured witness should be given due weightage and
should be relied upon; since his presence cannot be
doubted, unless there are major contradictions and
discrepancies and noticed a host of decisions to buttress this
position. Then, it was recorded that the learned Counsel for
the appellants, at the outset, conceded that the conviction is
not challenged and he only seeks application of the PoO Act,
since the appellants have not been convicted previously for
any offence. The learned Judge then went; according to us,
went overboard on an exposition of the law with respect to
the PoO Act and its application, as also Sections 360 and 361
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The impugned
order quotes copiously from the cited decisions and abruptly
finds application of Section 4 of the PoO Act on the finding
that the incident occurred in 2003 and the appellants have
suffered in the matter for the last 22 years, as also the absence
of criminal antecedents during these years, as informed.
While the conviction was affirmed, the sentence was
modified applying Section 4 of the PoO Act directing
personal bond of Rs.20,000/- each and an undertaking to

Page 5 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
maintain peace and good behaviour during a period of one
year.
7. Learned Counsel for the appellants pointed out that
the accused are habitual offenders, involved in many
criminal cases during the trial and the appeal. Even if the
offence charged in the instant crime was the first offence,
there is no application of Section 4 of the PoO Act. Learned
AoR for the State also alertly points out that the High Court
had not taken the report of the Probation Officer, and in any
event, the State had filed a counter-affidavit in the appeal,
specifically, bringing out the criminal antecedents as also
pointing out that the accused were recommended to be
detained as a preventive measure.
8. Learned Counsel for the accused, the 2
nd and 3rd
respondents, would however point out that the accused have
always been on bail and they are now aged above 60 years
and have a family to look after. Learned Counsel submits that
in any event if the impugned judgment is set aside, the
appeal must be considered afresh. Learned Counsel submits
that a remand may be made and the accused allowed to be
continued on bail. It is also pointed out that the victim is still

Page 6 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
alive and the appeal filed by the first informant is not
maintainable.
9. We are informed that the accused had not undergone
any sentence and was not in custody even for a single day.
We had called for the report of the Probation Officer, which
is placed before us. The criminal antecedents of the accused
are listed by the Probation Officer as below: -
'Criminal Antecedents of Accused Onkar Nath:
i. Case Crime No. 0382/2022, under Sections 147,
148, 323, 452, 504, 506 IPC & Section 7 of CLA;
Charge Sheet No. A-34 dated 23.01.2021; Status:
Pending trial before the Court.
ii. Case Crime No. 0383/2022, under Sections 147,
323, 352, 504, 506 IPC; Charge Sheet No. A-319
dated 18.12.2022; Status: Pending trial before the
Court.
iii. Case Crime No. 6028/2007, under Sections 147,
352, 379, 407, 452, 504, 506 IPC and Section 3(1)(x)
of the SC/ST ACT.
iv. Case Crime No.58/2003, under Section 308 IPC;
Charge Sheet No.25/2003
v. Case Crime No.651/2010, under Sections 323, 427,
504, 506 IPC; Charge Sheet No.21 dated
26.07.2010.
Criminal Antecedents of Accused Shiv Kumar:
i. Case Crime No. 112/2021, under Sections 147, 504
IPC; Charge Sheet No. 106 dated 18.07.2021;
Status: Pending trial before the Court.
ii. Case Crime No. 0382/2022, under Sections 147,
148, 323, 452, 504, 506 IPC & Section 7 of CLA;

Page 7 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
Charge Sheet No. A-34 dated 23.01.2021; Status:
Pending trial before the Court.
iii. Case Crime No. 0383/2022, under Sections 147,
323, 352, 504, 506 IPC; Charge Sheet No. A-319
dated 18.12.2022; Status: Pending trial before the
Court.
iv. Case Crime No. 6028/2007, under Sections 147,
352, 379, 407, 452, 504, 506 IPC and Section 3(1)(x)
of the SC/ST ACT
v. Case Crime No. 58/2003, under Section 308 IPC;
Charge Sheet No. 25/2003
vi. Case Crime No. 651/2010, under Sections 323,
427, 504, 506 IPC; Charge Sheet No. 21 dated
26.07.2010.'
10. More disturbing is the current status of the injured
victim, which has also been reported by the Probation Officer
in the following manner: -
i. The thumb of his right hand was found almost
completely severed from the palm, hanging
merely attached by a flap of skin. Deep,
traumatic injury scars were observed on the
back of his right palm.
ii. Prominent deep injury scars were observed on
the back of the left palm as well as the left wrist.
iii. Deep, lengthwise injury scars were present on
the lower part of the abdomen. In the central
lower abdomen, a large protrusion/outgrowth
of flesh and hanging lump was found, along
with another large lump on the right side of the
abdomen. The victim experiences acute pain
during movement, sitting, and standing, and is
compelled to continuously wear a broad
lumbar support belt.
iv. Deep, grave injury marks were observed on
the left side of the back of his neck.
v. Distinct injury marks were present on the right
shoulder, alongside sharp cut marks near the

Page 8 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
outer edge of the right eye and on the right
ear.'
11. Obviously, the incident has left not only its scars on the
victim but has left him, in the words of the Probation Officer,
'visibly weak, slow, sluggish and drowsy'. The victim also
'walks with great difficulty, suffers continuous pain, and has lost
substantial functionality of both upper limbs, right hand being
disabled'. The victim's family consists of six daughters of
which four are married and two unmarried. The victim's
medical treatment is continuing at Max Hospital, Lucknow.
These aspects more than explain why the victim is not before
us, and the first informant, his brother is before us seeking
justice to the victim.
12. We cannot but, with an amount of consternation, notice
the casual manner in which both the Trial Court and the High
Court considered the issue from the stage of taking
cognizance till the release of the accused on application of
the PoO Act.
13. The accused have gone scot-free without suffering a
single day of imprisonment, especially by reason of the
misplaced sympathy based on grandiose expositions of law;

Page 9 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
totally inapplicable to the facts of the case. Section 4 of the
PoO Act does not permit its invocation, when it is found that
the accused is a first offender. We also are unable to
comprehend as to why the High Court observed that the
accused were suffering for twenty-two years. True,
protracted trial is agonizing but here, the accused were on
bail and merrily indulging in criminal activities. The victim,
on the other hand, in the ensuing years was, day-in and day-out suffering the debilitating effects of the attack. The
circumstances of the case including the nature of the offence
and the character of the offender should be the reigning
factor in deciding as to whether it is expedient to release the
accused on the premise of good conduct; which in the facts
of this case is lacking. The brutality of the crime and the
grievous nature of the injuries sustained by the victim, ought
to have persuaded the Court to draw an adverse inference on
the aspect of 'nature of offence'.
14. Sub-section (2) of the PoO Act also requires that the
Court shall take into consideration the report of the Probation
Officer, if any, before making an order under sub-section (1).
Even if the report of the Probation Officer was not before it, it

Page 10 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
is pointed out in the counter-affidavit filed on behalf of the 1st
respondent, through the C.O, Bahraich, Uttar Pradesh, that
the prosecuting agency had filed a counter-affidavit on
14.07.2017, specifically bringing to the notice of the Court the
criminal antecedents of the accused. An application made by
the Superintendent of Police dated 20.12.2023 to the District
Magistrate to take action against the accused, was also
placed on record; a preventive detention measure. There
was a proposal to take action under the Uttar Pradesh Control
of Goondas Act, 1970, against the accused. The High Court,
despite the overwhelming adverse report on the 'character
of the offenders' and giving short shrift to the 'nature of the
offence', released the accused on good conduct. There was
nothing commending the Court to so release the accused,
since the conduct, over the years, of the accused was
anything other than 'good'.
15. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we set aside
the impugned order of the High Court. We direct that the
accused, the 2nd and 3rd respondents herein, shall surrender
within a period of two weeks of this order, failing which, the
Additional Sessions Court, Bahraich, which conducted the

Page 11 of 11
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl) Nos.6984-6985 of 2026
trial and convicted and sentenced the accused shall take
immediate proceedings to apprehend the accused.
16. The Criminal Appeals shall stand restored before the
High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow. We request
the High Court to take up the appeal only after ensuring that
the accused are taken into custody and then only the appeal
be heard.
17. The appeals stand allowed with the directions
hereinabove.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.
....................................... J.
 (J. B. PARDIWALA)
....................................... J.
 (K. VINOD CHANDRAN)
NEW DELHI;
OCTOBER 07, 2026.
